newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Hong Kong urged to safeguard post-1997 autonomy.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong urged to safeguard post-1997 autonomy.

text.p: Hong Kong will have to be ready to defend its promised autonomy after Beijing resumes control of the bustling entrepot in 1997, the territory's chief civil servant warned on Wednesday.

Hong Kong chief secretary Anson Chan told the National Press Club in Canberra she was confident the territory faced a bright future under the "one country, two systems" that China has pledged when the colony reverts from British rule in July.
But she warned there would inevitably be disagreements about the meaning of the concept, and the 1984 Sino-British Joint Declaration and Basic Law which set out the terms of the transition.
Chan, the first ethnic Chinese or woman to hold the post of chief secretary, said she expected business and foreign governments to press Beijing to honour its pledges.
"Above all, I think it is also up to the people of Hong Kong, and I include in that the business community -- we all need to be able and be prepared to stand up and defend our autonomy," she said.
"I don't think for a moment that simply because there are promises laid out in the Joint Declaration and the Basic Law that those promises will all be delivered intact," she said.
"We need to be able to articulate concerns, we need to defend our autonomy."
Chan said she believed Beijing wanted to honour its agreements with London.
"I do not have the slightest doubt that Chinese leaders are sincere about the autonomy promised to Hong Kong after 1997," Chan said.
"Nor do I have any doubt the Chinese leaders are absolutely committed to making the transition work," she said.
"I am not saying that after 1997 it will be plain sailing all the way. I don't for a moment believe that it will be that," she said.
"We will undoubtedly have our ups and downs in our relationship with China."
